subsection: 2. Stakeholder interaction, conflict and its resolution

notes.b: A business deals with its stakeholders (owners, investors, employees, consumers, suppliers, the local community and government, plus managers and interest groups) and they depend on each other. Each relationship can be co-operative, competitive or both.
points: Stakeholders rely on each other, so a conflict with one stakeholder has effects on others: for example, a dispute with staff can delay orders and upset consumers.
In a co-operative relationship, interests align. Owners and employees share a goal of growth, so both benefit when profit rises and the business expands.
In a competitive relationship, one group's gain is the other's loss. Owners want low wages to maximise profit while employees want high pay, so each gain for one reduces the other.
Most relationships mix both types, so the same pair can co-operate on product quality while competing over pay. Co-operative is not good and competitive is not bad.
Recognising the balance tells a business which relationships need protecting and which need careful management, before a clash of interests becomes a conflict.
notes.tip: If a case asks how stakeholders interact, show both the co-operative side and the competitive side. A common mistake is treating every relationship as conflict.

notes.h: Owners and employees: pay and working conditions
notes.b: Pay, hours and working conditions are a frequent source of tension between a business and its workforce. Each conflict below is built as cause, effect and how to avoid it, the three parts an exam answer needs.
points: Cause: a business under cost pressure may propose pay cuts or longer hours, while staff expect improvements as profits rise.
Effect: low morale, absenteeism, industrial action (such as a strike) and the loss of skilled staff, all of which reduce output and service quality.
Avoiding it: fair pay structures, clear communication about performance and profit, and regular consultation with staff, so that employees hear about decisions before they are made.

Resolving it: the Workplace Relations Commission offers free, confidential mediation for workplace disputes. For employment rights complaints it is offered only if both parties agree, as an alternative to adjudication.

If direct talks fail in an industrial relations dispute, the Labour Court can help. Its recommendations are not legally binding and cannot be appealed, so it is an independent third party, not a judge that orders a result.
notes.tip: To explain a conflict, give the cause and the effect on the business. Naming the issue (such as pay) without its effect is a common mistake in exam answers.

notes.h: Business and the community: planning and pollution
notes.b: A business affects the surrounding community through noise, traffic, emissions and changes to land use. People who live nearby have a say, so disagreements often arise when a business wants to grow.
points: Cause: a factory expansion may increase traffic and noise, or raise concern about waste discharged into a local river.
Effect: objections to planning applications (the request for permission to build), protests, damage to the firm's reputation and possible legal action by residents or authorities.
Avoiding it: consulting residents before a planning application, publishing environmental plans and investing in local facilities.

Sustainability: pollution, emissions and energy use are increasingly decided on sustainability grounds. South Dublin County Council refused a Google data centre extension at Grange Castle in August 2024 for insufficient grid capacity and too little on-site renewable energy. Google appealed and An Coimisiún Pleanála overturned the refusal with conditions.

A community objection can also succeed. At Killala, Co Mayo, An Coimisiún Pleanála overturned a permission granted by Mayo County Council after objections, finding the applicant had not shown enough grid capacity, on-site renewable energy or consistency with the Climate Action Plan 2025.
A third party who made a submission to the planning authority may appeal to An Coimisiún Pleanála within 4 weeks of the local authority's decision, so the community has a formal voice.
notes.tip: When a case is set in an environmental context, link your resolution to sustainable conduct and transparency, such as publishing environmental plans, not just to talks.

notes.b: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) is voluntary action by a business beyond what the law requires, and it is one of the main ways to reduce friction with the community.
points: CSR is voluntary, such as local sponsorship, whereas compliance is simply doing what the law requires. This is why paying a legal tax is not CSR.
CSR reduces friction with the community, but it works only when the business's conduct matches its stated commitments.
Greenwashing, claiming sustainability without conduct to match, damages trust, which is why honest CSR is an ethical commitment as well as a way of avoiding conflict.
notes.tip: Define CSR as voluntary and beyond legal requirements, and say it works only when conduct matches what the business claims.

notes.h: Business and consumers: price and quality
notes.b: Consumers judge a business by price, quality and fairness. Disputes arise when a product fails to meet expectations or the price seems unfair.
points: Cause: a faulty, misdescribed (not as advertised) or overpriced product generates complaints and demands for refunds.

Effect: lost customers, negative online reviews and possible action by consumer protection authorities. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) enforces consumer protection law in Ireland, but it cannot take cases for individual consumers.
Avoiding it: quality control, clear labelling, honest pricing and a complaints process that resolves problems quickly.
Transparency about sourcing and pricing protects trust in the brand, which is an ethical as well as a commercial asset.

Digital: social media and online reviews let a consumer complaint spread quickly. An online complaints form, e-mail updates and customer service chat let a business resolve problems before they escalate.
notes.tip: Say what action a consumer protection authority can take. Do not claim it takes cases on behalf of individual consumers.

notes.h: Business and suppliers: price and payment terms
notes.b: Suppliers want fair prices and prompt payment, while the business wants low costs and extended payment terms (the agreed time allowed to pay an invoice).
points: Cause: a business that pays late, or demands sharp price cuts, can strain a supplier's cash flow, the money coming in to pay its own bills.
Effect: a supplier may refuse future orders, raise its prices or withhold stock, which disrupts production.
Avoiding it: payment terms agreed in writing, regular reviews of prices and long-term supply partnerships, so both sides know what to expect.

The European Communities (Late Payment in Commercial Transactions) Regulations 2012 give a supplier the right to interest if a payment is late. Where the contract sets no date, the default is 30 days from receipt of the invoice.
The parties may agree longer terms, but terms over 60 days must be expressly agreed and not grossly unfair, so a business cannot simply impose very long waits.
Where a dispute arises, a partnership agreement can set volumes, quality standards and pricing rules that both parties accept in advance.
notes.tip: A sample business paying a supplier late is a typical case. Give the effect on the supplier and then on the business's own production.

notes.h: Investors and management: risk and dividends
notes.b: Investors want a return on their money and may accept risk differently from managers, who may prefer to reinvest profit in the business.
points: Cause: managers may want to keep profit for expansion, while investors want dividends (a share of profit paid out) now and may distrust risky projects.
Effect: pressure from shareholders, calls for changes in management, and a loss of investor confidence that can lower the share price.
Avoiding it: clear reporting of performance, an agreed dividend policy, and open communication about strategy and the risks it carries.
notes.tip: State both sides of the clash: investors want income now, managers want growth later. Then give the effect on the share price.

notes.h: Business and government: tax and regulation
notes.b: Government sets taxes and regulations that businesses must follow, and businesses may seek lower taxes or lighter rules.
points: Cause: a new environmental or employment regulation adds costs, which the business may see as excessive or unfair.
Effect: lobbying (trying to influence government decisions), delayed investment, and penalties or enforcement action where rules are broken.
Avoiding it: keeping up to date with changes in law, taking part in public consultations, and building compliance into everyday operations.
Formal legal routes, such as the courts, also exist for resolving these disputes.
notes.tip: Show how a new regulation affects costs, then give an avoiding method such as taking part in a public consultation.

notes.b: Resolution methods range from direct talks to the involvement of an outside party. The choice depends on how serious the conflict is and whether the parties still need each other.
points: Negotiation: both sides discuss their positions and aim for an outcome each can accept. It is quick and cheap, but may favour the stronger party.
Compromise: each side gives up part of its demand, so neither gets everything it wanted. It is the outcome of a negotiation, not the talking itself.
Mediation: a neutral third party helps the parties reach their own agreement without deciding the outcome for them. It suits parties who still need each other, but needs both to agree.

Partnership agreement: a written arrangement between a business and another stakeholder that sets shared goals, responsibilities and procedures for settling future disputes. It is not the legal form of a business partnership.
When direct talks fail, an independent body can help, such as a mediator or a state body like the Workplace Relations Commission or the Labour Court.
notes.tip: For discuss or evaluate, weigh two methods against each other, for example negotiation against mediation, and link each to its effect on the business. Do not mix up mediation with a decision made by a third party, because the mediator does not decide.

notes.b: The best option is to prevent a conflict. Avoiding happens before a problem arises, while resolving happens after, and a business that avoids conflict saves the time, cost and damaged relationships of resolving it.
points: Communication and consultation: telling stakeholders about decisions and asking for their views early, for example e-mail updates to staff or an online consultation with residents.
Corporate social responsibility: voluntary action such as local sponsorship builds goodwill, provided conduct matches commitments.
Fair contracts: fair pay for staff and written payment terms for suppliers remove the main causes of dispute before they start.
Shared goals: agreeing common aims, as in a partnership agreement, turns competing interests into co-operation.
Transparency: honest pricing, open reporting to investors and clear sourcing information protect trust, an ethical commitment that prevents conflict.
Sustainability: choosing sustainable conduct, such as using on-site renewable energy, avoids the objections that stop community and environmental projects.
notes.tip: When asked to suggest ways of avoiding conflict, choose the method that suits the stakeholder and say why it works, for example consultation for staff and transparency for investors.

keyTerms.definition: A relationship between stakeholders in which their interests align and each benefits from the other's success.
A relationship in which one stakeholder's gain is another's loss, such as when higher wages reduce profit.
A clash of interests between stakeholders that arises when one group's goals or gains limit another's.
Discussion between parties aimed at an outcome both can accept, reached without outside decision-making.
A settlement in which each party gives up some of its demands in order to reach agreement.
A process in which a neutral third party helps disputing parties reach their own agreement.
A written arrangement setting shared goals, responsibilities and procedures for resolving disputes between parties.
A business's voluntary commitment to act ethically and contribute to society beyond what the law requires.
The agreed period and conditions within which a buyer must pay a supplier's invoice.

factCards.term: Typical cause of owner and employee conflict
factCards.definition: Pay, hours and working conditions pulling in opposite directions.

factCards.term: Results of conflict with the local community
factCards.definition: Planning objections, protests, reputational damage and legal action.

factCards.term: Three ways to avoid consumer disputes
factCards.definition: Quality control, honest labelling and fair pricing, backed by a fast complaints process.
Late payment and sharp price cuts that strain the supplier's cash flow.

factCards.term: What investors and managers disagree over
factCards.definition: Paying dividends now or reinvesting profit for growth.

factCards.term: Common cause of business and government conflict
factCards.definition: A new regulation or tax that adds costs the business sees as excessive.
The parties keep control of the outcome, so they are more likely to accept it.

questions.prompt: Identify two potential conflicts between a supermarket and its suppliers, and suggest appropriate ways of avoiding and resolving each.
questions.model: The first conflict concerns price and payment terms. If the supermarket demands sharp price cuts or pays late, the supplier's cash flow is strained and it may refuse future orders. To avoid this, the supermarket can agree payment terms in writing and review prices regularly. If a dispute arises, the parties can negotiate, or they can sign a partnership agreement that sets prices and volumes in advance. The second conflict concerns quality and delivery. If the supplier delivers goods that do not meet the agreed standard, the supermarket may reject them and the supplier may lose the contract. The conflict is avoided through clear quality specifications and shared goals, such as consistent supply. If the matter cannot be settled between the parties, a mediator can help them reach their own agreement.

questions.prompt: Explain how a co-operative relationship between owners and employees can benefit a business.
questions.model: When owners and employees share the goal of growth, employees are more willing to commit effort and to accept changes that improve productivity. This raises output and the quality of the product, which increases sales and profit for the owners. The shared interest also reduces the likelihood of industrial action, which would otherwise disrupt production and lose orders. A business benefits from this stability because it can plan investment and meet deadlines with confidence.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between mediation and negotiation as ways of resolving a dispute between stakeholders.
questions.model: Negotiation is direct discussion between the parties, who work towards an agreement without an outside person involved. Mediation adds a neutral third party who helps the parties communicate and reach their own agreement, but who does not impose a decision. The third party's role is what distinguishes mediation, and it is often used when the parties cannot make progress on their own.
